title: Why I Support the Common Core
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart explains why a teacher who dislikes standards in general still supports the Common Core, grounding the case in classroom experience rather than testing. His first reason is that the standards call for challenging all students with complex texts; he recounts a wasted year on a remedial program and a freeing mandate to grow his students however he could. His second reason is that they require students to argue, write, and discuss around those texts while building real knowledge of the world. His third is that they prepare every student for college and work, debunking the myth that some students will not need those skills. He ends with the caveat that he still does not love standards.
points: Students far below grade level should still be taught grade-level complex texts, with the teacher as the key scaffold.
The author's regret over a remedial program shows that low expectations, not student capacity, were the problem.
Reading comprehension depends on background knowledge, so the standards' emphasis on knowing about the world is welcomed.
Skills with complex text and evidence-based argument are needed by all students, not only the college-bound.
quotes: One of my great regrets as an educator is the year I wasted teaching remedial students with the remedial Language! program that my district spent millions on. (We didn’t call them remedial classes; they were “accelerated”).

I felt terror because I could no longer blame a bogus curriculum for bad results, yet I was thrilled because I already knew that my students were capable and longing for so much more. I knew that, even though my students were allegedly the antithesis of their peers in “Gifted and Talented” classes, they could handle GT-level challenges.

Surprisingly, the second prong of my approach did not foment a revolt from my low reading level kids (at least, not for long). This is because there was a key resource in the room that enabled them to cope with complex texts: me.

In other words, even if a student enters ninth grade with a fourth grade reading level, he should still be taught how to grapple with a book like Bradbury’s Fahrenheit 451. If this sounds cruel to anyone, that’s because you might undervalue the power that a teacher can have in helping students learn to read texts that are well above their reading levels, and you also might undervalue a kid’s desire to leap over a high bar.

Oh, and towards that end, kids are expected to know stuff; knowledge about the world is a key part of the CCSS. By the grace of God, education is moving away from treating reading comprehension like something that happens within a vacuum. We’re done pretending that a kid from rural Wyoming can comprehend a story about sailing with the same ease as a kid from Salem.

The CCSS debunk the myth that if a student is not “the college type,” he/she will not need skills similar to those required by a college-bound student. The person who can’t read complex texts, who can’t make evidence-based arguments, who doesn’t know how to listen and speak and use language effectively within a variety of settings isn’t ready for college or work: he/she is just screwed.
